messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details:
- What the test does:
  - Chooses a time zone different from the system default (anotherZone).
  - Builds a Calendar in anotherZone.
  - Builds a SimpleDateFormat with pattern "h:mma z", sets its time zone to anotherZone, and formats cal.getTime() to produce the expected string, which includes the time zone name for anotherZone.
  - Uses FastDateFormat.getInstance(pattern).format(cal) to produce the actual string and asserts equality.

- Relevant code flow in FastDateFormat/FastDatePrinter:
  - FastDateFormat.getInstance(String) delegates to a cache with (pattern, null, null). Passing null for time zone causes the cached instance to be bound to the system default time zone (this is the established behavior in Commons Lang’s caching layer).
  - FastDateFormat’s constructor wires a FastDatePrinter with the time zone provided (default if null).
  - FastDatePrinter.format(Calendar) calls format(calendar, StringBuffer), which calls applyRules(calendar, buf), iterating mRules (compiled from the pattern) and appending to the buffer via Rule.appendTo(buf, calendar).
  - For the 'z' pattern (time zone name), the corresponding rule uses the printer’s stored time zone (mTimeZone) to obtain the display name, not calendar.getTimeZone().

- What goes wrong:
  - The Calendar passed into FastDatePrinter.format(Calendar) is in anotherZone, but the 'z' rule ignores the calendar’s time zone and uses FastDatePrinter.mTimeZone instead (which, because the instance was obtained with getInstance(pattern) and no explicit time zone, is the system default).
  - As a result:
    - Time fields (h, mm, a) are taken from the provided Calendar and therefore reflect anotherZone correctly.
    - The time zone name (z) is taken from mTimeZone (system default), not from calendar.getTimeZone(), so the suffix is the default zone’s name.
  - This mismatch causes the test to fail: the printed time looks correct for anotherZone but the zone name is for the default zone.

- Why this aligns with the bug report:
  - The report states that FastDateFormat’s "z" pattern does not respect the time zone of Calendar instances passed to format(), printing the machine’s default zone name instead. That is precisely the behavior caused by the 'z' rule consulting the printer’s stored time zone rather than the calendar’s.
  - The mention that the issue arose around the work to support parsing (LANG-462) is consistent with a refactor where the time zone name rule and its caching keyed off the printer’s configured time zone, inadvertently ignoring the calendar’s.

- Root cause:
  - The rule that handles the 'z' pattern (time zone display name) in FastDatePrinter uses the printer’s configured time zone (mTimeZone) to compute the display name, instead of using the Calendar’s time zone from the Calendar argument supplied to format(..). This makes format(Calendar) produce a time zone name tied to the FastDateFormat instance’s (default) time zone rather than the calendar’s time zone.

- Impacted behavior:
  - format(Calendar) with a Calendar whose time zone differs from the FastDateFormat instance’s time zone (including the default) will print an incorrect zone name for 'z'. Other fields still reflect the Calendar’s zone because they are pulled from the Calendar’s fields directly.

- Expected fix direction:
  - In the 'z' handling rule, derive the TimeZone from the Calendar passed to appendTo(..) (i.e., calendar.getTimeZone()) and use that when looking up the display name (and any internal caching) so that format(Calendar) respects the calendar’s time zone.
